Video Beat: Toasting Babylon 5

VIDEO BEAT: TOASTING BABYLON 5 article by Christalene Loren Science fiction programs have traditionally been a bane for television networks. Such shows often require elaborate visual effects shots created either by photographing models with a motion control camera and compositing the images together, or by using computer generated graphics on highend equipment. Either way, science fiction is extremely expensive to produce; and with few exceptions, producers avoid it like the plague. All that changed, however, when the two-hour television pilot for Babylon 5 aired in February 1993. Babylon 5 marked the first time that the lowend Video Toaster was used to create a major portion of the visual effects for a broadcast television production. 'We originally bid the job of the space station for Babylon 5 as a miniature," noted visual effects supervisor Ron Thornton. "We had calculated that it would take us six weeks with a crew of six to eight people, plus $10,000 to $15,000 for materials. But we never purchased the materials. I had an Amiga 2000 computer; and when I put it together with a Video Toaster - which became available in 1990 - I was able to build a space station inside the computer in just two weeks." Most of the show's spaceships were designed on a single Video Toaster/ Amiga 2000 system. "I was living next door to Paul Beigle-Bryant at the time," Thornton recalled. "We knocked a hole in the wall between our two apartments and networked our computers together with cable." As the project expanded, Thornton established his own visual effects company, Foundation Imaging, to handle the workload for the pilot program, which included fifty-two effects shots and various display screen imagery. In addition to Thornton as visual effects supervisor, the team included Beigle-Bryant, the company's system specialist designer, and in-house producer Shannon Casey who worked to bring the project in on time and within budget. To create the spacecraft and galactic vistas for Babylon 5, Foundation Imaging introduced Video Toaster technology to series television. Prior experience in lighting models enabled Thornton to give the computer generated space hardware a photographic look. "I always wanted to see crisp and colorful effects in a space show, instead of just dull gray spaceships. What I wanted was something organic, but without the nightmarish Giger look. The alien ships, for example, were inspired by squid, jellyfish and flower shapes." While Thornton occupied himself with designing the effects, Beigle-Bryant kept the computer system from crashing. Although mainframe computers had been linked together for years, Beigle-Bryant was one of the first to network microcomputers, designing software that enabled eight Video Toasters to talk to each other. "I set up the system like a parallel graphics computer," Beigle-Bryant recalled. "While I employed 'CanDo' - a general purpose authoring system - to modify some of the software, most of the time I wrote in 'ARexx', which is the computer language used to control the Amiga software. We had eight Amigas - each with 32 megabytes of RAM - for rendering, with a central service computer sitting in the middle collating the whole thing. For the pilot, we used an IBM PC server with five gigabytes of disc storage. I glued it all together to prove it was possible to do high-end graphics using commercially available, medium-end technology." The closing shot in the Babylon 5 pilot illustrated the vast capability of the fledgling company's Toaster technology. Beginning with a view from outside the space station looking at crew members visible through a window, the camera appears to zoom back from twenty-five meters away to a distance of some fifty kilometers. "You could never build a model or a motion control track to simulate that distance," said Thornton, "so, instead, we used the live-action footage of the crew members and matted that onto a polygon, placing it behind the model. The rendering system incorporated the liveaction plate into the computer model of the receding space station so that as we appeared to move away from the model, the plate action was CINEFEX 57 • 11

scaled accordingly." In September 1993, Foundation Imaging won an Emmy for its visual effects work on the Babylon 5 pilot. Currently, the company is producing deepspace imagery for the twenty-two shows scheduled to air during the 1994 season. Although they continue to employ the 2000 Amiga/Toaster system to generate these effects, their operation is now twice as large. "We have gone from a two-man to a fourman animation crew," noted Beigle-Bryant. "There are sixteen Toasters rendering during the day and twenty-two at night. We have also upgraded to a 15-gigabyte DEL XE 4000 server that runs twentyfour hours a day, seven days a week. With the server, we can move across platforms, because PCs, Amigas and Macs all see the same files, and this enables us to do our own equivalent of Harry work in-house. If the tool does not exist on the PC, then it exists on the Mac or the Amiga." Animated effects for the series, such as laser beams and weapons fire are done on a Macintosh by animator Kevin Kuchaver. "Kevin takes Exabyte tapes of the rendered shots and prints out key frames on his laser printer. He then rotoscopes on top of those images and, using standard animation techniques, pencils in the laser beams 12 • CINEFEX 57 and scans them back into the computer as elements to be composited together." Although most of the show's effects shots are exteriors, Thornton and his crew have also created non-anthropomorphic extraterrestrials for episodes where the use of an actor in a suit was not an option. Working with John Vullich and Everett Burrell at Optic Nerve - who do makeup effects for the series - they built a three-tentacled creature called a Na'Ka'Leen feeder for an upcoming episode. "John and Everett sculpted a six-inch-tall clay maquette of the creature and made a database for the shape of the body," Thornton said. "Then we scanned images of the maquette to make the texture maps. In Jurassic Park, ILM actually painted the CG dinosaurs in 3-D; but we couldn't do that with our system. So we used a technique to cheat in the texture surfacing. We transformed the creature so that we were able to open it out flat. Then we planar-mapped it and transformed it back into its original shape. This allowed us to go all the way around the creature without the texture map streaking through it." A single tentacle, used for closeups, was the only full-size model built for the project. " A longer version of the tentacle was also built into the comBoth space hardware and organic alien lifeforms were produced on low-end computer systems. puter," noted Thornton. "During the live-action, we shot a cardboard cutout of the creature on the set for lighting reference and to determine size relationships between the creature, the actors and surrounding objects. Then we constructed, in the computer, a simplistic version of the sets and set dressing pieces used in the shot. We applied this information as a database to help with motion tracking - which frequently had to be done whenever the creature made contact with the ground to ensure that the three tentacles did not slide backwards on the surface. This was necessary because the Video Toaster's 3-D software - Lightwave 3.0 - does not have inverse kinematics." A major challenge was in compositing the alien creature with the background elements. "We spent a lot of time working with the level of focus on the creature to get it just right," Thornton explained. "By taking the creature out of focus and rotoscoping in some foreground elements where the actors walked in front of it, we were able to create the illusion that it was interacting with them. That was more effective than having shots that cut from person to creature and creature to person." Another technique used to heighten realism was to adjust the image sharpness. "Sometimes the computer can make images that are a little too crisp," explained Thornton. 'When that happens, we have to go in and soften them so that they match the look of film. We also have to maintain motion blur in all of the shots. This was done by re-rendering at the subframe level. We rendered seventeen versions of the creature between frame one and frame two. These renderings were all overlaid with a certain amount of transparency to create a blurring effect. It was timeconsuming in terms of rendering, but it made an enormous difference in the finished product. Without motion blur, the creature would have looked like a stop-motion puppet, with that same strobing feel Having discovered the practicalities of using lowend computer graphics for television, Thornton sees the potential for a major thrust in terms of future programming. "The novelty of just being able to do this type of work with computers is now over and done with. Everyone can now settle down and start to do the best possible work with the system we are using. If what we are doing becomes the trend, then soon you really will not be able to believe anything you see on your television screen."

SPECIAL VENUES: DEEP EARTH, DARK RIDE article by Mark Cotta Vaz People crowd a subway platform awaiting the subterranean shuttle. Once inside the craft, bound for the mysterious Crystal Caves, they are piloted by a personable on-board computer and treated to exterior views of their fantastic journey transmitted via videocam to a large monitor within. At points in the trip, darkened shutter windows open to allow passengers firsthand glimpses of the subsurface world through which they are traveling, images of tranquil beauty interrupted by heart-stopping lava flows, earthquakes and other dangers. Such is the scenario of 'Deep Earth Exploration,' a featured attraction at Las Vegas' newest casino resort, the MGM Grand Hotel. Midland Productions of Richmond, California, creators of the attraction and veterans at creating simulation rides, see the 'Deep Earth' experience as an innovation in the basic movie-and-motion illusion of most simulator rides. "One of the problems of simulator rides," explained company producer Yas Takata, "is that oftentimes it's difficult to sustain the illusion that a ride vehicle has actual moving or flying capability, because you've had to enter a movie theater or you never see the vehicle because you'd notice all the hydraulics. What's unique about 'Deep Earth' is that it has both a dark ride - like Disney's 'Pirates of the Caribbean' or 'It's a Small World' - and a simulation." The illusion begins when patrons enter the bustling Deep Earth' subway station platform. Ten twelve-passenger vehicles - called gopher shuttles' - load up with passengers and accelerate into an excavated tunnel. "When the shuttle greets the passengers at the boarding area," noted Midland director Don Fox, "they see a video camera setup on the shuttle instead of a window. The preshow narrative tells them that because of the dangers involved. they cannot be allowed to look out a window, but Modelmaker Elliot Fan dresses a subterranean miniature constructed for Deep Earth Exploration® - a combination dark ride and simulator attraction created by Midland Productions for the MGM Grand Hotel in Las Vegas. 16 • CINEFEX 57 will see the world through videocam transmissions." As the vehicles depart the station, opaque shuttle windows close and passengers must focus their attention on the interior video screen. Along the six-minute journey, the screen imparts images of a dizzying descent through tunnels of earth and ice, brushes with a netherworldly creature, and perilous escapes from lava flows and an earthquake, with each ride vehicle's hydraulic simulator providing the corresponding shakes and rolls. At a predetermined juncture - when a story point allows for a calmer moment - the video screen goes black, and the shutters along the sides open to reveal threedimensional sets. "The screen goes black for several reasons," Fox explained. "First, it would have been very difficult to match the film exactly to the sets. Second, we didn't want to dilute the riders attention. When the video is on, we want people focused on the screen; and vice versa for the sets. Every time the shutters open, the audience enters a dark-ride environment, seeing fire or ice or crystals in threedimensional sets that go back fifteen feet with parallax views." Ultimately, the psychology of 'Deep Earth Exploration' is for riders to connect the simulator action and the dark-ride set environments into one seamless experience. "Hopefully, people won't know where the film ends and the sets begin," said Takata. "Even though the ride vehicle actually moves at a constant foot-a-second along an approximately three-hundred-thirty-foot circular course - and you're only traveling an average of forty-five to sixty feet between events - the simulation makes it seem as if you've traveled miles. With the magic of film, we can travel a thousand miles an hour." Working closely with Duell Corporation of Los Angeles on the design, and with AVG of Los Angeles which constructed the sets, Midland storyboarded the look of the miniature filmed environments with an eye toward ensuring that they could also be exe-

cuted on a larger scale. "Fortunately, we were not limited by the motion the platform was capable of producing," noted Takata. "Had that been the case. I think we would have had to design the ride with the emphasis on the platform. What's interesting is that with a good film, we can exceed the limits of the platform. Most platforms can't go upside-down or drop ninety degrees straight down - but if the film is effectively executed and planned, a few subtle motion cues can fool people into thinking that they're doing things the platforms couldn't possibly do." Midland created 'Deep Earth' with a melding of miniatures and postproduction computer graphics - a process the company has named 'Flow Motion.' The models would be shot upside-down, allowing for lighting and access, and the footage would be digitally flipped, with the space left by the open area filled in with computer graphics of flowing lava and water. The process required a year of development with a crew of fifteen led by Fox and Takata. "We built all of the sets at Midland," Takata recalled. "Each was sixty feet long, made of typical plaster, chicken wire, wood and paint. Joel Hladecek, our director of photography, programmed the motion control camera to travel the length of the model, simulating the POV of the 'gopher shuttle' craft." Director of computer graphics Steven Horowitz developed a proprietary system to digitize threedimensional points. He substituted a custom sensor in place of the motion control camera and altered Camera assistant Matt Kwan readies a motion control camera for an underground shot inside the main switching platform set. Hladecek's program to sample where the computer generated liquids would hit the tunnel walls. "First, software was developed that simulated the motion control camera flying down the tunnels," explained Horowitz. "Using move and point data, we created a numerical mesh which followed the model contours on which we texture-mapped animated water and lava provided by RenderMan shader expert Mitch Prater. The liquids and their mattes were rendered to match the point of view at which the models were photographed. The liquids and miniature shots were then composited digitally. It was an extremely tricky process because the tolerances were in tenths of inches and halves of degrees." Key to the simulation aspect of the attraction was the programming of the motion control platform to match the moves of the film. The platform had hydraulic actuators and three degrees of freedom, each of which was controlled by a computer. "Trey Stokes was the on-site motion programmer," noted Takata. "Programming the simulators is kind of a black art and took quite a bit of time. A lot of people think all you have to do to get a realistic move is take the motion control data from the camera and play it into the data on the platform. But when you get into it, you find out that you really need to try different things until you get something that feels just right. If it's not perfect, if the visual cue is not synced up to the motion cue, then your brain tells you something's wrong and the manifestation of that is a serious headache." Takata sees a big future for simulator and dark ride attractions, despite competing entertainment choices on the horizon. "People are predicting that simulator rides will fail as virtual reality comes in. However, one of the variables that virtual reality hasn't been able to address is 'throughput' - the ability to entertain large numbers of people. Virtual reality allows you to enter a computer space and manipulate it; but so far, it's a one-man/one-time experience. With simulators, we can take groups of people and run them through; and if it's done effectively, it can feel like a virtual experience. "Takata sees future simulator rides utilizing large-format films and moving into huge warehouse spaces for the sets - like Deep Earth, only on a much larger scale. "It would be a fantastic experience. I hope they become part of the next generation of theme park entertainment." CINEFEX 57 • 17

Video Beat: Order Out Of Xaos

VIDEO BEAT: ORDER OUT OF XAOS article by Kevin H. Martin When, after years in development, the Sci-Fi Channel finally debuted in late 1992, its broad mix of specialty programming - fantasy, science fiction and horror ranging from major motion pictures to long-defunct television series - demanded a station opening which reflected this diversity. "It wasn t going to be just another movie service," director Scott Miller explained. 'The Sci-Fi Channel would be a sort of continuum, an environment where you could find an extraordinary array of some of the most imaginative and entertaining programming ever created. Our goal was to visually characterize these qualities in the opening. " To this end, Miller developed a nonterrestrial fantasy environment featuring a bizarre world teaming with intricate spacecraft and mysterious energy bubbles. Also featured would be a brief 'birth of the universe' extrapolated from current scientific theory. "The idea was for a big, exotic, slightly retro mini-epic, played out in its entirety in less than one minute." To accomplish this task, Miller and Sci-Fi Channel producer Paula Brown selected Xaos, a San Francisco computer graphics firm with a flair for surrealistic imagery. A supplier of graphics for MTV, NBC and Fox, Xaos has also contributed to the feature film The Lawnmower Man and to numerous commercials. Company art director Mark Malmberg was pleased by the opportunity to participate creatively in the evolution of the Sci-Fi Channel spot. 'When Scott came to us, he had already started some of the spaceship design work, and he brought with him an orthographic map illustrating the kinds of elements he thought might be included on the journey. So we worked together to really develop the concept further, prior to storyboarding the whole spot." Miller and Malmberg's approach was deliberately low-key, emphasizing subtlety through tantalizing glimpses of the bizarre planetscape. "We enjoy developing scenes that have a high level of detail Energy bubbles containing iconic imagery drift through space in the 'Big Bang' promotional spot created by Xaos for the Sci-Fi Channel. - images that lend themselves to repeat viewings without becoming repetitious, that do not necessarily use the 'punch-in-the-face' approach. For us, it's a matter of developing the atmosphere of a given scene." That sense of atmosphere is present from the start, as a computer generated Sci-Fi Channel logo, animated by Henry Preston, appears against a strange and stormy background. This segues directly into the 'Big Bang' - a sequence illustrating the Xaos view of how computer graphics can best be employed. "The industry presently seems to be concentrating on 'photorealism," Malmberg observed, "but this notion is based only on what a camera can capture on film - which is a very limited perspective when it comes to reality and what actually comprises the viewing experience. We have a greater interest in creating an artistic representation of a given scene. Consequently, we found ourselves wondering: 'What does the birth of a universe look like?' and How would you portray such an event in just a couple of seconds instead of the billions of years it would really take?** Xaos' vision of the Big Bang features flaming debris blasted outward from a flaring colorburst. "We wanted to do more than just the big white flash you always see on space shows. To create debris trails and the look of the rocks that go hurtling past, Tony Lupidi combined 3-D geometry with image processing. " Also used was Xaos' proprietary 'Warpo' software - roughly the computer graphics equivalent of image-distorting mylar - to create rippling, dimensional variations among the fiery trails. Another Warpo' transition - together with a soft circular wipe - takes viewers from the birth of the universe to one of the strangest worlds ever seen. "We wanted to do a segue that didn't draw too much attention to itself, but which still suggested a certain passage of time since this planet came into being long after the Big Bang actually took place." The viewer is then taken on a swooping aerial tour of the world, flying first through a crevasse and then CINEFEX 57 • 21

emerging well above a mechanized cityscape set perpendicular to the camera's orientation. "Scott thought that would be fun. In the crevasse you think everything looks pretty normal; but then you emerge into the real world and find that it's set ninety degrees from what it ought to be. The whole thing is very much in keeping with the idea of a 'sci-fi' setting." To create the detailed landscapes and refinerylike installations encrusting them, Xaos enlisted the model department and motion control facilities at Apogee. "Since this was just about the last job Apogee took before disbanding," Malmberg noted, "the model shop had already broken away as a separate business under the name Grant McCune Design." Considerable sweetening was needed to link the model elements into the rest of the computer graphics piece. "At Apogee, I would have as many as nine different passes done on some of the shots, which allowed us to have mattes for areas where the CG ships would come out from behind the rocky landscape. Additionally, we used special lighting passes which, during post, we were able to utilize on the Harry to create the glows around electrical plants in the crevasse. There were phosphor light passes, glow 22 * CINEFEX 57 light passes and shadow passes as well, all done to maximize integration of CG with the model." Malmberg managed to take advantage of the multiple channels available in the digital realm for storing different types of information on threedimensional relationships between objects and the camera. "In addition to the red, blue and green channels, there is an alpha channel, which is typically used for matte or transparency data in compositing. We use this channel - and others, if need be - for storing different types of 3-D information about the objects in the image. To truly integrate these elements, we needed an atmosphere that would work dimensionally within the planet's environment. We didn't want a flat fog effect with things getting duller and fainter as they got further away. Instead, we used particle systems to create mists that moved through space independently and dimensionally." For the spaceships seen flying along the horizon, Miller provided basic blueprints to Xaos, which then subcontracted the construction of wire-frame computer models to Viewpoint Animation Engineering of Utah. Catching the camp classic on video in 1988 - thirty years after its inauspicious theatrical release - Dougherty was immediately taken with the movie's basic premise, and with its inherent possibilities as a modern-day remake. Not surprisingly, Dougherty found few others who shared his enthusiasm. Tepidly received by the public in its day, Attack of the 50 Foot Woman had been poorly conceived and executed, even by Even so, Dougherty was impressed enough with the concept to try to generate interest in a possible remake. Nobody seemed to get it. "I showed the movie to producers I was working with at the time," Dougherty recalled, "and I met with nothing but blank stares." His enthusiasm undampened by the lackluster response, Dougherty proceeded to write a screenplay on spec - adapted freely from the Mark Hanna original - which he subsequently shopped around the film industry. But even with his concept updated and assigned to the printed page, there were no takers. "Nobody wanted to make it as a feature; so it quickly became a writing sample I would show to get other projects." A turning point for the Attack of the 50 Foot Woman remake came with the success of a Dougherty script entitled Lovecraft, which Home Box Office made into the noirish occult thriller Cast a Deadly Spell. When the screenplay was nominated for the first Ray Bradbury Award, HBO asked Dougherty - who already had a Tony and an Emmy - if he had any other scripts to show them, and the writer promptly pulled out Attack of the 50 Foot Woman. HBO responded favorably, "At the time, which was two years ago, nobody else was doing remakes like this; and I think that made HBO all the more enthusiastic about it." Agreeing to produce the movie as one of its first-run features for the Fall 1993 season, HBO secured the rights to the film and assigned Allan Arkush to direct, with Dougherty acting as executive producer. During the initial development phase, however, Arkush left the project, which then went into developmental limbo until it resurfaced a year later with Christopher Guest as director and Debra Hill as producer. Like the original Attack of the 50 Foot Woman, Dougherty's script centered on Nancy Archer (Daryl Hannah), an unhappily married woman who has a close encounter with an alien spaceship. Though shaken by the experience, she suffers no apparent physical effects until later at home when she becomes angered by her philandering husband, Harry (Daniel Baldwin), and her domineering father (William Windom). In a sudden emotional outburst, Nancy grows to gigantic proportions, literally 'going through the roof due to hormonal changes inflicted upon her by those inside the flying saucer. With her dramatic increase in size, Nancy's personality also undergoes a metamorphosis, and she gradually changes from an emotional marshmallow to a woman who is unafraid to throw her now-considerable weight around. "People think she's a threat because she learns to stand up for herself," stated Debra Hill. "Her physical growth works wonderfully as a metaphor for a repressed woman who grows inwardly as she grows in size. This naturally brings her into conflict with the men who have always dominated her life." As the project moved into production, one of the primary concerns was finding a company to produce the film's more than two hundred effects shots, ranging from optical split-screens to traveling mattes to forced perspective miniatures - even some digital work. "Gene Warren's name came up right away," Dougherty recollected. "His company, Fantasy II, had created a giant clown for Killer Clowns From Outer Space. It was done as a forced perspective miniature and it looked terrific. So that shot, coupled with Gene's experience, made Fantasy II our first choice for the effects." Agreeing to come aboard, Fantasy Il was faced with the prospect of fitting a big-screen effects profile into a small-screen budget. The film's entire production budget was only $7 million - hefty for a television movie, but meager compared to the budgets enjoyed by most feature effects projects, especially considering the volume of effects work called for in the script. "I can't think of another television movie that has had as many effects as this one," Gene Warren observed. "We created more than two hundred shots for Attack of the 50 Foot Woman - approximately the same number of shots that were in Honey, I Blew Up the Baby, which was a $35 million movie!" An Academy Award recipient for his work on Terminator 2, Warren devised an effects approach that utilized a number of vintage techniques often overlooked in the quest for the latest in effects technologies. "We wanted to avoid the split-screen look, with the big woman always on the right and the little guy on the left. That becomes pretty obvious, especially with lengthy sequences such as the ones in this movie. For the longer scenes, it became cost-effective to construct a miniature, take it on location, raise it up in the air, and tie it in as a forced perspective shot. It gave us a different look than if we'd tried to do everything with split-screens or bluescreens." "The methods Gene employed really complemented the style of film I wanted to make, "Dougherty commented. "For me, this picture was about going back to the movies I grew up with; so I didn't want CGI characters or digital effects. I wanted to return to a simpler, more theatrical style of filmmaking, and Gene helped us to accomplish that." While enthusiastic about the opportunity to resurrect some of the older techniques that are rarely implemented in current effects films, Warren found little inspiration in the illusions created for the original 1958 movie. "I took one look at the original and then forgot about it," Warren said. "The film was worse than low-budget; it was no-budget. There were very few effects, and the technical level was very low because Nancy was just doubleexposed into the film. They tried to keep her against dark backgrounds so it wouldn't be obvious, but any time she walked in front of anything that had exposure on it, you could see right through her. If you were to hard-wrap that gunpowder with tape, you would contain it and thus create a bomb; but when it's left loose in the plastic bag, it just ignites itself and creates a quick flash that ignites the gas - which ignites the bomb. QUICK CUTS: DIGITAL EFFECTS article by Dale Kutzera When Paramount Pictures greenlighted the first Addams Family feature they could not have guessed that among the assortment of delightfully eccentric family members, one of the most popular would prove to be a disembodied hand called Thing. But where the original picture and its recent sequel, Addams Family Values, differed from their television predecessors was in their approach - creating a fully realized character in Thing through a combination of old and new effects techniques. Before a specific approach could be planned, effects supervisor Alan Munro met extensively with director Barry Sonnenfeld and producer Scott Rudin to discuss the exact nature of Thing. "I think the reason I got the job," remarked Munro, "was that I was the first person who actually had a point of view for Thing as a character rather than just an effect. The script initially called for Thing to perform such activities as combing Morticia's hair or helping Granny in the kitchen by stirring a pot. My feeling was that such actions - which defied gravity by requiring the hand to hang in midair - would kill the effect; because no matter how seamlessly you removed the body from the hand, you would still have the sense that there was an arm attached." Munro also felt it was important to impart a certain amount of grace to Thing's movements, avoiding those actions which appeared clumsy. "That immediately eliminated a whole lot of activities. When we tried, for example, to have the hand pick up objects and walk with them, we found it looked too awkward." With these general ground rules in place, the search began for an actor with a particularly graceful and photogenic right hand. "It was one of the most memorable and hilarious experiences of my life," Munro recalled. "We decided to audition dancers and magicians as well as commercial hand models, but what we ended up with was the most bizarre collection of humanity one might ever see. We had guys coming in with little faces painted on their hands, or little hand costumes: some even introduced their hands with pet names. Then Chris Hart auditioned. Chris had gorgeous hands - very large with long graceful fingers - and he was the only one who demonstrated that innate sense of character we were looking for." Originally, Munro proposed dressing Thing in a standard dress cuff, the end of which would be black, leaving the stump to the viewer's imagination. The final design came from Richard MacDonald, production designer for the first film. The length of the stump was based on both practical and aesthetic considerations. "Extending the wrist a bit gave us a few more options," noted Munro. "The stump served as a big tail that stuck up in the air, enabling us to impart a greater sense of shifting balance. The other consideration was the practical limitation of fitting mechanics for an animatronic hand - which we knew we would need - into such a small space. The wrist gave us additional space in which to store batteries and things." The animatronic puppets, created by Dave Miller, were employed in the first film for activities such as massaging Gomez's head or pulling a wagon. More involved sequences, however, used a 'live' hand and optical matting. For each shot, two takes were filmed - one with Christopher Hart as Thing and another from the same locked-down position without the actor. These foreground and background plates were then sent to Visual Concept Engineering for optical compositing. In fast-paced scenes - where standard matting techniques would have erased the blur of the actor's rapidly moving fingers, creating a choppy, chattery look - intricate splitscreen mattes were created. These encompassed the entire hand and immediate background, yet still removed the image of the actor's arm from the liveaction plate. "The splits would change constantly throughout the shot based on the actor's position in In the two Addams Family films, the dexterous disembodied hand - Thing - was enacted most often by an actor, outfitted with a prosthetic wrist stump, whose real wrist and arm were either concealed from view or eliminated optically with split-screens and rotoscoping. the live plate," explained VCE president Peter Kuran. "Since the eye is naturally drawn to a straight line, we would hide the splits in contours where they were broken up and couldn't be detected. The only thing that had to be rotoed frame by frame was the part of the stump wherever it crossed through the split line." Another technique used to maintain blur in the finger movements involved creating two mattes of slightly different sizes. "Normally when you make mattes, you print the male matte from the female or vice versa," Kuran noted. "In this case, however, there were different sets of mattes for male and female. The clear center matte was larger to allow for the blurs, and the black center matte was smaller so that the blurs would double-expose over the background plate. It worked best when the object was shot against a darker background." Further complicating the process, split-screens and outline mattes were occasionally featured in the same shot. While split-screens were used to insert the hand into the background plate, outline mattes CINEFEX 57 • 73

The camera was either locked down or mounted on a computerized motion control system to repeat precisely a given movement, take after take. Everything had to be laid out with great precision. We would take one shot to a certain point, and then have to switch to another angle to have him finish turning around." For the sequel, the problem was resolved by creating a computer generated stump. Obviously, at some point the actor's real arm would have been in the way, so we turned to computer animation." Sequences chosen for digital matting typically involved Thing interacting closely with other characters. Rather than cut out Hart's hand and paste it into a separate background element, the computer animator could digitally paste portions of the background element over the actor's body. "It's more easily accomplished on computer because you have an invisible blend. You can cut a piece out of one shot and paste in a piece from the other shot without having to worry about One practical-type effect used in the first film but abandoned in the sequel entailed having Hart stick his hand through a hole in the set or table. "My sense was that every time we did one of those shots in the original movie," Munro observed, "something about it looked like there was somebody sitting under the table - even though we always made sure to show the audiences that no one was there." Such shots were also arduous for Hart who, during one scene in the original film, found himself in a tight, uncomfortable position underneath the floor. "It took forty-five minutes to dress the floor around his forearm. So even before cameras rolled, Chris' hand was tired and cramped. Then he had to do all this extremely rigorous, complicated stuff, picking up golf clubs and flicking golf balls around. Fortunately, Chris had an unbelievably good attitude about it, which was a significant factor in making the Thing character work." After three years of nonstop involvement in bringing the bizarre character to life, Munro is still experiencing residual effects. "This project depended on a lot of nonverbal communication. We weren't just doing a hand, but a hand without a body attached to it. So the gestures weren't supported by facial expressions or anything else. When I first began working on The Addams Family, I found myself obsessed with hands. Even today, in restaurants, at meetings or parties, I still find myself watching what people are doing with their fingers. Maybe twenty years from now I'll wake up and find myself looking at feet."

COMMERCIAL SPOT: CHEVY HULK article by Jeff T. Miller Poised majestically on a bluff overlooking Lake Powell is a jet black pickup. "This is the last 1993 Chevy S-10 ever to be built," a voice-over intones. As the camera closes in, the truck comes alive; door handles clacking, dials and controls moving on their own. Suddenly, the sound of rending steel is heard as the vehicle's metal skin bursts open and peels back. Windows and instrument panels explode in a shower of glass and plastic. Rent body panels drop away, exposing a smoother, sportier, more rounded form beneath. When the metamorphosis has run its course, the black pickup is gone and in its place is a sleek new, bright red '94 model. The commercial is Chevrolet's introduction to its 1994 series of S-10 pickups. Seeking to unveil the new product line in a visually dynamic way, the automotive giant enlisted the help of Boss Film Studios of Marina del Rey to create seven commercial spots for the trucks. Helming the effort was Terry Windell, a Boss Film resident director equally at home with live-action and visual effects. Working closely with director of photography Bill Bennett, Windell made the decision early on to accomplish as many effects shots as possible without the help of computer graphics, relying instead on the grittiness and complexity of live-action physical effects. Computers would be used only later to massage the imagery during postproduction. One of the most effects-intensive of the spots - a commercial nicknamed 'The Hulk' - opens with a beauty shot of the '93 Chevy accomplished with a Hothead mounted on a Louma crane. "The concept," said Windell, "was to start with the '93 black truck which then rips open to reveal the brand new red model. Graphically, I thought that was very interesting." As the camera moves in, the door handles begin clacking and dials begin spinning. "In the vein of Das Boat, I had the dials and lug nuts pop On stage at Boss Film Studios, director Terry Windell lines up a shot on a Chevrolet S-10 pickup during production on a series of commercials touting the year's new models. off. Rather than using a morphing technique, we installed air bladders in the seats to make them swell, with tear-away material rigged to split and rip apart at the seams." As the camera cuts to the outside, the truck literally begins to burst out of its skin as the metal tears open. Working hand in hand to realize the pneumatic and mechanical effects for the sequence were physical effects technician Bill Klinger, miniature supervisor David Jones and chief engineer Andres Bustanoby. Lug nuts were cast in plastic and blown off their bolts with the aid of compressed air. Fiberglass molds were taken from a '93 Chevy S-10 and lead foil resembling cold rolled steel was pressed into them. Shaped like body sections of the '93 model truck, the foil was then painted black and hung on cut-up pieces of the red '94 successor. "It looked essentially like a big Swiss-cheese truck," observed Windell. Project crew chief Alan Faucher devised a way of using air mortars hidden inside the truck, along with fine steel wires and air rams, to tear the foil. Laced onto the back side of the lead foil, the steel wires were connected to the air rams. "When the switch was flicked," explained Windell, "it was like a pulltab kind of gag. The wire was actually glued to the back of the foil in a zigzag pattern, protruding at the initiation points. It was then attached with more wire to the ram so that when the ram pulled it, it would zip along that pattern like a jagged zipper, opening up the lead foil. This was timed very closely with the air mortars which would immediately blow open the side. They would actually blow away several pieces that were pre-scored. We did a series of tests to determine how big the sheets should be that were rigged to blow away, and how much air would be needed." The effect also called for an extensive amount of CINEFEX 57 • 79

rotoscoping. "The idea was to use red as the chromakey color," Windell explained, "because of the red color of the underlying truck. But with all the holes for the rams, wire gags and air mortars, there were too many areas that would not self-matte or key; so an awful lot of hand rotoscoping was required." In order to slow down the peeling metal effect in real time, the sequence was shot at frame rates ranging from 48 to 360 frames per second. 'We used several different cameras," noted Windell. "Here at Boss we have several modified pin-registered cameras which are based on Mitchell cameras. For the ultra-high-speed 360 frames per minute, we used Photosonics cameras. All shot 35mm film." One difficulty the effects team encountered using foil to simulate steel was that as the foil blew open, occasionally it would begin to fall back into 80 - CINEFEX 57 place before the entire section could complete its rip. To resolve the problem, certain pieces of the action were played up to a point and then areas of the frame were frozen, allowing the rest of the action to continue. "In postproduction," Windell elaborated, "Alan Barnett of Side Effects would carry the animation to a point of my choosing, and hold it in sections. Essentially we were splitting the scene into anywhere from three to a dozen pieces, putting different holds and freezes into different areas in order to maintain the illusion that what was tearing was steel." An additional problem arose from the basic differences in shape between the '94 and the '93 model trucks. Since the '93 model was boxy compared to the more fluid body style of the '94, there was a concern that there would be large gaps of For a spot in which a 1993 truck rips apart to reveal a 1994 model, Windell and crew used mostly physical effects to achieve the illusion. negative space as the '93 truck was torn away. To alleviate this problem, the computer graphics department was enlisted to digitally compress the '94 truck into the foil shell. "We took the '94 truck," explained Windell, "and using computer graphics imaging, squished it into the shape of the '93. The effect is very subtle - because we didn't want to see any morphing - but while the shell is ripping away, underneath the '94 is sliding into position in its true form. It probably happens in twelve frames or less - which is very quick - so you don't notice that we've actually played with the shape of the truck and then brought it into its own form." Inside the truck cab, a new dashboard thrusts its way up through the old dash. "The dashboard was molded and reconstructed in plastics," Windell noted. "It had a battering ram - another pneumatic gag in the shape of the center section of the new dashboard - and it was painted chroma-key blue. As the new dash smashed through the old '93 dashboard, it became a self matting shape." The '94 dashboard was registered and shot on a separate pass to match the motion of the chroma-key blue plug. Then it was put together digitally by Barnett at Side Effects, where the compositing for the commercials was accomplished. While the beauty shots of the trucks were done on location, effects work was shot in studio on sets built and designed by Michael Hartog. Great care had to be taken to match the shots. This was accomplished partly by using a series of huge backings, about 40 by 170 feet in size. Also employed were intermediate or 'middleground' cutout set pieces to represent the buttes of Lake Powell, as well as threedimensional foreground set pieces. The different trucks were registered to each other using a video switcher. The entire commercial was transferred to digital tape and composited on a Quantel Harry. All matte work was accomplished digitally. "In retrospect," observed Windell, "I'm thankful that I have an optical background and have done a lot of bluescreen work, because with bluescreen you learn how important it is to be meticulous about how you work with things and light them. But the digital aspect really opens up your lighting capabilities even more, and in the process gives you greater latitude in terms of mattes and superior edge quality. The results can be quite spectacular." SHEY

VIDEO BEAT: McCARTNEY TAKES WING article by Mark Cotta Vaz When Paul McCartney wanted to fly like a bird for the music video title cut of his new album Off the Ground, the legendary rocker tapped Industrial Light & Magic to do the honors. For McCartney, impressed with some ILM effects magic for a British Petroleum commercial widely broadcast in the United Kingdom, the video would be his first work with the effects house. For ILM, accustomed to big-movie budgets and high-end technology, the challenge was to produce high-quality work within the expected constraints of a lower-budget music video production. The ILM Off the Ground team included director Matthew Robbins and visual effects supervisor Scott Squires, both veterans of the British Petroleum ad that had originally caught McCartney's eye. "Paul wanted to fly, but exactly how to accomplish it, and the story structure, were basically up to the director and ILM," said Squires. To keep costs down, stock aerial footage would be combined with normal bluescreen wire-rig flying, with the composite work accomplished on Macintosh computers using special software. "ILM had used Macs on the Young Indiana Jones television series primarily for matte paintings, but doing all the compositing and post work on a Macintosh at that time was pretty unusual for this type of project at this level of sophistication. With the Mac, we had more control than was available from a Harry or some of the other post tools people usually use: plus it was more cost effective. We did all the compositing with a program I wrote called 'FlipBook, ' which allowed us to do bluescreen composites, extractions and manipulations on the Macintosh at full video or film resolution. We went ahead and did the wire removal on Silicon Graphics machines in the digital department because they were set up to do that." Off the Groundopens with McCartney alone in a San Francisco recording studio - a dressed Legendary rock star Paul McCartney sought out Industrial Light & Magic to produce a music video for the title track of his Off the Ground album. set created from scratch at George Lucas' pastoral Skywalker Ranch north of the city. The familiar city Skyline visible through the mock-studio window was actually a Translite photo blow-up positioned outside and backlit with soft lights. A magical gust of wind blows through the studio, and McCartney is lifted from his prone position atop a piano and carried out the window, soaring over green fields and forests, castle ruins and rivers, through clouds and past a hot air balloon. "Paul had very specific ideas about the flying," stated Squires. "He didn't want to simply jump up like Superman and take off; he wanted to be lying down and, like a bird, flap his wings or do some vibrating of the hands to get himself aloft." Once the appropriate stock aerial footage had been obtained, timing and synchronization points were worked out for the matching bluescreen wire work which would be filmed on an ILM stage. "We had a really primitive means of mocking up the shot," noted Squires. "We fed a video tap to a monitor, with a video camera positioned some ten feet away. Then we mixed the two signals of the background plate and the video signal of Paul flying around. The video cameraman could pan and tilt and move on Paul relative to the background imagery, and that material was combined with the background plate in video, just as a rough, to check the overall action and lighting and timing." Two traditional flying harness rigs were used for McCartney - a fiberglass belly-pan covering the front part of the stomach with wires coming off four separate points, and a canvas waist harness with two wire points on each side to allow for somersaults, spins and other acrobatic moves. Most of the flying was accomplished with the belly-pan, the fiberglass shell of which was created from a mold taken off McCartney's body. Advised to be in shape for the physical demands imposed by the flying rigs, McCartney took to his training with such gusto that CINEFEX 57 • 85

in the several months between the mold-taking in England and his flying at ILM, the rock star had dramatically trimmed and tightened his stomach muscles. For a belly-pan shot of McCartney lifting off from his piano, the harness - which no longer fit his new physique - had to be altered by skinning off a thin layer of fiberglass. "We suspended Paul in front of the bluescreen about five to six feet in the air above a blue pad for safety," said Squires of the intense, one-day shoot. "We had wind machines going and different types of lighting depending upon the background plate that we were matching. In some cases we had the lights moving a little to give the sense that McCartney was going through different changes in light. If he started to roll, he'd get lit from the opposite side. We wanted to photograph him close to full-frame so we'd be starting with the best quality image. We also wanted to shoot him making the tilts, rolls and different perspective changes himself. Once we worked all the timings and synchronization points on stage with the video, we could do his dips and dives to correspond relatively with the background plates. The sizing changes could then be done afterwards in the post process. Upon completing the bluescreen photography, we telecined that footage as well as 86 - CINEFEX 57 the background plates - whenever we work on commercials and videos and have to marry multiple images, we transfer from film to video with frame registration. Then we transferred from the D-1 images to Exabyte tapes - which are 8mm videotapes used as digital storage in special computer drives. These tapes were read into a Macintosh computer. Most of the cameras used to shoot the aerial stock footage had been nose-mounted; so in a number of cases we ended up reversing the backgrounds so we could have Paul flying towards camera and the background going away." With the Macintosh and Squires' FlipBook software, a number of skillful manipulations were accomplished. For an interactive shot of McCartney dipping his hand into a body of water, a bluescreen shot of the flying musician was composited into the background plate. Milk was mixed into the water used for the shot to help the droplets stand out against the bluescreen. "On the Mac," said Squires, "we could color and balance him, resize images, tweak the contrast ratio, soften the edges of the mattes as need be, and generally do as much as we could to try to incorporate him into the background scenes. Although most of the shots of Paul were fullframe, one scene - where he was flying over trees Director Matthew Robbins confers with McCartney on set prior to a bluescreen flying shot. in a foggy environment - required a tight shot. In doing that, we found that if we rotated or moved him slightly down in size, we would lose part of his arms and he would be cut off at the elbows. So in FlipBook we cloned from existing arms and added to the missing areas." The postproduction work also required adding a scene of McCartney and his guitar flying out of the recording studio window. "Originally, the shot had the guitar floating out the window, then it cut to McCartney flying around," Squires explained, "but the producers felt they needed something to make it clear to the audience that Paul begins his flight by first going out that window. So we took some footage we had shot of him going away and we matched the move on what we had done with that image to the shot of the guitar floating out the window. We composited him on top of that. Then we were able to paint the guitar back in with Paul in front so that it appeared to follow him out the window." For the finale, McCartney's guitar, hat and band members join him off the ground, with any telling wire work digitally removed using ILM's in-house computer graphics. In the final shot, McCartney and his band rise out of frame with only their feet appearing above a view of the San Francisco skyline and a twilight pastoral landscape - duplicating the Off the Ground album cover. "We shot bluescreen of Paul and some stand-in legs to represent the band members who had already returned to England at that point," Squires recalled. "We matted the legs against the Translite of the city. We wanted to duplicate both the front and back of the album cover, which had the feet dangling above the landscape with a sunset on the front and a twilight sky with stars on the back. So we dissolved from the Translite of San Francisco to the album cover background. The album, of course, was square; so we had to compress some things and shift our crop area to include the stars. Still, it was a pretty close match." For ILM's Off the Ground team, the video project was a rare and enjoyable opportunity to work with a living legend. McCartney, too, enjoyed the experience, reveling in his newfound powers of flight. "Paul got a big kick out of flying," remarked Scott Squires, "and even tried some somersaults and acrobatic stuff. Unfortunately, we didn't have any background plates to incorporate it into. I think he took the flying harness back to England for some future project."

LASERDISC REVOLUTION: COPPOLA'S KANE column by David C. Fein Crimson dreams of erotic obsession and love eternally entwined with the lust for blood - such visions are the essence of Francis Ford Coppola's contribution to the legacy of the notorious Count Dracula. Striving to embrace the Bram Stoker source novel, and walking in the footsteps of Orson Welles - clearly the road less traveled - Coppola has conjured a film destined to survive as a piece of cinematic history. Bram Stoker's Dracula, like Citizen Kane, conveys more in the design of a single shot than most movies communicate in entire scenes. Fittingly, both The Voyager Company and Columbia/TriStar Home Video have recognized the artistic significance of the film with special edition laserdiscs featuring supplemental behind-thescenes footage. In actuality, there are three laserdisc releases, each presenting the film in its proper aspect ratio of 1.85:1. The two from Columbia/TriStar offer a transfer of the film in CLV format, but their special edition ($49) - priced ten dollars higher than the basic, movie-only version - includes the film's two theatrical trailers and a documentary. The Voyager Company's Criterion Collection release ($125) features a transfer superior in both sound quality and image, and is presented in CAV format to better facilitate frame-by-frame examination of the film's artistic merits. As with the majority of Voyager releases, the Dracula laserdisc provides a commentary track and a separate music and sound effects track. Featuring director Francis Ford Coppola, visual effects supervisor Roman Coppola and makeup supervisor Greg Cannom, the commentary is packed with interesting insights and anecdotes, including an extensive discussion of how the film's intentional 'old-fashioned' quality was achieved not merely through its art direction, but also its photographic technique and special effects. For example, the production utilized Director Francis Ford Coppola works with his actors in staging a confrontation between Dracula - in his bat form - and the stalwart Van Helsing in Bram Stoker's Dracula. a hand-cranked camera to lend a period look to the establishing shot of Dracula (Gary Oldman) prior to his initial encounter with lost love Elisabeta in the form of Jonathan Harker's bride-to-be Mina Murray (Winona Ryder). For similar reasons, it was decided that wherever possible, special effects sequences would be shot in-camera so as to avoid the more contemporary look afforded by bluescreen and digital effects - both of which were eventually employed, though sparingly. Hanging miniatures, forced perspective, matte paintings, in-camera matting and a plethora of mechanical effects were also used to complement the film's period look. The Criterion supplement opens with an outline of the Dracula legacy, beginning with the first known tragic vampyre poem, The Giaour, written in 1813 by Lord Byron. It continues with a history of the Bram Stoker novel, recounting the difficulties Florence Stoker experienced fighting the German company PranaFilm over its production of Nosferatu, the unlicensed adaptation of her late husband's source novel. Though the negative and all prints of the film were ordered destroyed by the courts, the F.W. Murnau film survived, and is today considered one of the masterpieces of German expressionism. Completing the history is a list of thirty-six Dracula films Voyager considers the most memorable. Immediately following the retrospective is the first theatrical trailer for Coppola's ostensibly faithful recounting of the Stoker tale. As stylish as the production itself, it features rivulets of blood streaming together to form the title, intercut with flashcuts from the film. The next chapter is essentially the Dracula article which appeared in Cinefex. While many of the Cinefex stills have been included, they are reduced to about one-eighth the size of the screen and consequently lack any discernible detail. As discussed in the commentary, many of the design elements of Bram Stoker's Draculawere inspired by certain classic films and expressionistic art. In the chapter on artistic influences, Voyager has mounted an intriguing montage demonstrating the impact on the film of such cinematic classics as Nosferatu and Jean Cocteau's Beauty and the Beast, 92 - CINEFEX 57 followed by still frames of eight inspirational medieval paintings. An even more in-depth examination occurs in the chapter on the Eiko Ishika costumes which Coppola considered integral to his visual concept for the film. Included are printed interviews with the costume designer and director, plus a wealth of designs, and stills of the finished work. During preproduction, the entire film was storyboarded and edited on video, with detailed narration, enabling Coppola to visualize its flow prior to shooting a single frame of film. Once filming began, he would replace a completed sequence's storyboards with the day's best takes, allowing him to Gary Oldman, in old-age makeup, as Dracula in the opening Transylvania sequences. examine his progress at any time during production. In the first of two chapters covering this approach, dozens of storyboards are presented sequentially frame by frame. While most of the storyboards are of sequences that appear in the final cut, sketches of Dracula's unfilmed attack on the sailors are also included. The next chapter further defines this videobased filmmaking process by presenting the initial meeting between Dracula and Professor Abraham Van Helsing (Anthony Hopkins) as it progressed from edited storyboard to final videotape edit. Unfortunately, the completed sequence as it appears in the film is not offered. Another sequence is featured in the form of an 'editing workshop.' Most, if not all, of the takes in which Jonathan Harker (Keanu Reeves) bids goodbye to Mina in preparation for his departure to Dracula's castle are presented as shot. Viewers can choose their favorite takes and program their laserdisc players to assemble the sequence in literally hundreds of possible combinations, affording first-hand experience in the art of motion picture editing. Following the exercise - and for the purpose of comparison - the sequence is repeated as it appears in the film. With a Voyager Criterion edition of Bram Stoker's Dracula available to the consumer, one might wonder what additional materials the Columbia/TriStar special edition could contribute. Their version offers both theatrical trailers plus a complete half-hour documentary produced originally for Home Box Office. (Voyager's offers only the first trailer and a ten-minute excerpt from the HBO program.) The second theatrical trailer is noteworthy for its greater number of scenes, including several alternate takes. The documentary, Blood Lines: Dracula the Man, the Myth, the Movies, is an entertaining and thorough examination of Coppola's process of preproduction readings, rehearsals and planning, featuring behindthe-scenes footage and interviews with filmmakers and cast members. At one point in the narration, Coppola remarks that over the next few years, he believes audiences will re-examine Bram Stoker's Dracula and discover many of the artistic elements showcased within its design. With the film enjoying a spot in Voyager's prestigious Criterion Collection, as well as a Columbia/TriStar special edition, there is ample opportunity for film aficionados to do just that by exploring fully the enduring quality of its stylish visuals and special effects.
